questions.q: Where does Northbridge's azurerm backend store Terraform state?
options: In a local .tfstate file committed to the storefront repo
As a blob in the sttfstatenorthbridge storage account, in the rg-tfstate resource group
In the Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server
In Azure Key Vault alongside the other secrets
questions.explain: The backend.tf block points at resource group rg-tfstate and storage account sttfstatenorthbridge, container tfstate, with state stored as a blob there.

questions.q: How are dev and prod Terraform state kept separate within the same storage account?
options: They use different Azure subscriptions entirely
They use different blob keys (dev.terraform.tfstate vs. prod.terraform.tfstate)
Dev state is deleted after every apply
Prod state is stored in a different container only
questions.explain: Both environments share the same resource group, storage account, and container; only the state blob's key differs, keeping their state files isolated.

questions.q: Two engineers run terraform apply against the dev resource group within minutes of each other. What actually happens?
options: Both applies succeed and the state file silently merges their changes
The second apply fails to acquire the state lock and reports who is holding it
Terraform deletes the dev resource group to avoid ambiguity
The first apply is automatically cancelled in favor of the second
questions.explain: The azurerm backend uses an Azure Storage blob lease as a distributed lock. The second apply can't acquire the lease and fails immediately, naming the lock holder.

questions.q: What Azure Storage mechanism does the azurerm backend use to implement state locking?
options: A blob lease
A SQL transaction
A DNS TXT record
A role assignment
questions.explain: The azurerm backend acquires a blob lease on the state file during plan/apply operations, which functions as a distributed lock.

questions.q: Without remote state locking, what would have likely happened in the two-engineer collision scenario?
options: Nothing different — Terraform always serializes applies automatically
Both applies would read the same stale state, compute conflicting diffs, and one would silently overwrite the other's state
Azure would reject the second apply at the API level regardless of Terraform
The Postgres Flexible Server would fail to provision
questions.explain: Without a lock, concurrent applies operate on stale local copies of state and one engineer's changes can silently overwrite the other's record of reality, causing drift that's much harder to diagnose than a locked blob.
